sentences.text: Here's a question that sounds simple.
Five clinics send their patients home. Some of those patients are back in hospital within thirty days. Which clinic is doing the best job?
Each chip is one patient. A filled chip is a patient who was readmitted.
The obvious move is to count. At Alder, 13 of 30 patients came back: that's 43%.
Birch, 47%. Cedar, 40%. Dune, 58%. And at Elm, nobody at all.
Line them up from lowest to highest, and we have a league table.
Elm in first place, Dune in last, and Alder just ahead of Birch.
It looks like an answer. But for those two, the table has it backwards.
Welcome to Model in Motion, where we build statistical models one moving piece at a time.
This is the start of a new story: how to compare providers fairly. Today, unfair comparisons, and what a fair one would need.
Let's look more closely at Alder and Birch.
So far, we've treated every patient as interchangeable. They aren't.
Some are frail, or going home after a long and complicated stay. Patients like that are more likely to come back, wherever they're treated.
Let's mark those higher-risk patients with a ring.
Now sort the chips: lower-risk patients on the left, higher-risk on the right.
Look at who each clinic is caring for. At Alder, 24 of the 30 patients are lower-risk.
Birch is the mirror image: 24 of its 30 are higher-risk.
This is a clinic's case mix: the kind of patients it serves. And these two could hardly be more different.
So let's compare like with like, starting with the lower-risk patients.
At Alder, 8 of 24 were readmitted: one in three. At Birch, 1 of 6: about 17%.
For these patients, Birch does better.
Now the higher-risk patients. Alder: 5 of 6, or 83%. Birch: 13 of 24, or 54%.
Birch does better again.
Lower-risk patients do better at Birch. Higher-risk patients do better at Birch.
And yet, put everyone back together, and it's Alder with the lower rate.
Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic. This is Simpson's paradox, and it lies in wait wherever groups with different mixes are compared.
Here's what's going on. Give each clinic a beam, marked from zero to one hundred percent.
Each group of patients sits on the beam at its own readmission rate.
A clinic's overall rate is the point where its beam balances. And that depends on how much weight sits at each end.
Alder's patients are mostly lower-risk, so its balance point sits near the low end: 43%.
Birch's piles both sit further left: lower rates in both groups.
But most of its weight is at the higher-risk end, and that drags the balance point up to 47%.
So a raw rate blends two things: how well a clinic performs, and who walked in the door.
Here's a way to feel the difference. Imagine the two clinics traded patients.
Alder's two rates stay where they were. But now it carries Birch's patients, and its balance point slides all the way up to 73%.
With those same patients, Birch managed 47%.
And Birch, with Alder's easier mix? Its balance point falls to 24%, where Alder had 43%.
Whichever set of patients you choose, Birch comes out well ahead. The league table had these two the wrong way round.
Two clinics could be a fluke. So let's zoom out to 200 providers.
They're simulated, which means we know how good each one truly is.
Line them up from truly best on the left to truly worst on the right.
Then lift each one by its raw rate: lowest at the bottom, highest at the top.
If raw rates told the truth, the dots would hug the diagonal. Instead, they're scattered almost everywhere: a rank correlation of just 0.16.
Cut the table into fifths, and 142 of the 200 providers land in the wrong one.
Now re-sort the very same providers by how sick their patients are.
There's the pattern the raw rates were following all along: a correlation of 0.58.
There's a second problem in that league table, and it has nothing to do with case mix. Look at the two extremes.
Dune's 58% rests on 12 patients. Elm's perfect zero, on 11.
So try an experiment. Suppose all five clinics were secretly identical: every patient with the same four-in-ten chance of coming back. Now deal out the luck. And again. And again.
Even the bigger clinics wobble. The smallest swing much further.
So before trusting any gap between providers, we'll have to ask how much of it chance alone could produce. That question gets an episode of its own.
Let's gather it up.
A raw rate blends performance with case mix.
Compare like with like, and a ranking can flip.
And small providers swing with chance.
What we really want is to compare providers as if they had all treated the same patients.
With one risk factor, sorting chips into two piles was enough. But real patients differ in dozens of ways at once.
So next time, we'll build a single ruler for risk: a way to turn everything we know about a patient into one probability.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
